name: Saccharomyces ferment
summary: Yeast-fermentation filtrate used in essences like SK-II Pitera; the brand story is well known, direct trials are almost absent.
lead: Saccharomyces ferment is a cosmetic ingredient name for the filtered product of yeast (Saccharomyces) fermentation, used in essences and serums. The best-known branded example is Pitera, the yeast-derived ingredient in the Japanese skincare line SK-II.

name: Kombucha ferment
summary: Tea or plant extract fermented with a kombucha culture; only lab-dish antioxidant data exist for skin.
lead: Kombucha ferment is a skincare ingredient name for products made by fermenting tea or plant extracts with a kombucha culture (a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, often called SCOBY). Kombucha as a drink is a lightly sweetened fermented black tea, thought to have originated in China.

name: Tremella mushroom
summary: Snow fungus polysaccharide marketed as a hydrator; support is patents and reported claims, not trials.
lead: Tremella fuciformis, known as snow fungus or silver ear, is an edible white gelatinous fungus cultivated commercially in China and used in Chinese cuisine and traditional medicine. Extracts, especially polysaccharides, appear in skincare products from China, Korea and Japan, where they are marketed as moisture-retaining and anti-wrinkle.

name: Mugwort
summary: Artemisia herb used in K-beauty as a calming botanical; folk use is long, skin trials are absent and pollen allergy is common.
lead: Mugwort is a common name for several aromatic Artemisia species: Artemisia vulgaris in Europe, and A. argyi (Chinese mugwort) or A. princeps (Korean ssuk, Japanese yomogi) in East Asia. It has a long history in folk medicine, food, and moxibustion, and extracts are used in Korean skincare marketed as calming.

name: Houttuynia cordata
summary: Fish mint extract ("heartleaf") in K-beauty toners; cell data are encouraging, human skin trials are essentially absent.
lead: Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint, heartleaf or chameleon plant, is a perennial native to Southeast Asia used as a vegetable and herb in Vietnam, Japan, Korea, northeastern India and southwestern China, and in traditional Chinese medicine. Its extract, marketed as "heartleaf", is a prominent ingredient in Korean skincare toners, serums and sheet masks.

name: Ginseng root extract
summary: Korean-herb root extract sold as an antioxidant skincare ingredient, with no trials of its topical appearance effects.
lead: Ginseng root extract is a preparation made from the root of Panax ginseng, a perennial herb native to mountainous parts of Korea, northeast China and the Russian Far East that has long been used in East Asian folk medicine. In skincare it is used as an ingredient in K-beauty and herbal products, where it is marketed mainly as an antioxidant or soothing botanical; one US-listed topical product containing it is a herbal medicated soap.

name: Portulaca oleracea
summary: Edible succulent weed used as a soothing skincare botanical, backed by lab and animal data but no skin-appearance trials.
lead: Portulaca oleracea, commonly purslane, is a warm-climate succulent annual eaten as a leafy vegetable in the Mediterranean, Middle East, Asia and Mexico and used in folk medicine in many countries. In skincare, extracts appear in soothing and moisturising products; one DailyMed-listed essence combines Portulaca oleracea extract with niacinamide, glycerin and lotus flower extract.

name: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract
summary: Chinese skullcap root extract used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening ingredient, with small trials registered but little published human evidence.
lead: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract comes from Baikal skullcap, a mint-family plant whose dried root (huangqin) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine. Its main flavonoids include baicalin, baicalein and wogonin. In cosmetics it is used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening botanical.

name: Perilla seed extract
summary: Seed extract from an Asian culinary herb, used as a plant omega-3 skincare ingredient with no human appearance studies.
lead: Perilla seed extract is derived from the seeds of Perilla frutescens, a mint-family annual used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds contain roughly 38 to 45 percent oil. It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 or antioxidant ingredient.

name: Camellia japonica extract
summary: Japanese camellia botanical used in some cosmetics, with one mouse study and no human data.
lead: Camellia japonica extract is derived from the Japanese camellia, a flowering evergreen tree or shrub; its leaves can be made into tea and are reported to contain anti-inflammatory terpenoids such as lupeol and squalene. It is used in some cosmetics as a botanical ingredient, and Korean patent filings from 2004 and 2005 describe cosmetic compositions using it for anti-ageing, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes.

name: Hemp seed oil
summary: A fatty-acid-rich plant oil used in moisturisers and body care; the skin-specific evidence is thin.
lead: Hemp seed oil is a plant oil pressed from the seeds of low-THC varieties of Cannabis sativa. It is used as a food oil, in body-care products such as soaps, shampoos and moisturisers, and in industrial products such as paints and finishes. It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.

name: Volcanic ash
summary: A sebum-absorbing mineral in some K-beauty masks; the sources found describe the geology, not any skin benefit.
lead: Volcanic ash is fine fragmented rock, mineral crystal and volcanic glass, under 2 mm in diameter, produced by explosive eruptions. Its chemistry varies with the magma type, from silica-poor basaltic to silica-rich rhyolitic ash.

name: Witch hazel extract
summary: The classic astringent toner botanical; lab data exist, human skin trials do not.
lead: Witch hazel extract is a preparation made from the bark and leaves of Hamamelis virginiana, a shrub native to eastern North America. It is best known as the astringent 'witch hazel' sold as a skin toner, a product made by distilling the plant material in dilute alcohol.

name: Pine bark extract
summary: A polyphenol antioxidant supplement (Pycnogenol); studied for many conditions, not for appearance.
lead: Maritime pine bark extract is a dietary supplement made from the bark of Pinus pinaster, consisting mostly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins). Pycnogenol is a trademarked standardised version containing 70% procyanidins. It is sold as an antioxidant and is included in some supplement and skincare products.

name: Mistletoe extract
summary: A mistletoe botanical used in some skincare; its research is in cancer care, not skin.
lead: Mistletoe extract is prepared from European mistletoe (Viscum album), a semi-parasitic plant. Standardised or proprietary extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary cancer treatments, mainly in German-speaking countries, and the plant also appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products.

name: Noni fruit extract
summary: A Pacific fruit extract sold as an antioxidant; skin evidence is lab-only and liver-safety concerns are documented for oral products.
lead: Noni fruit extract comes from Morinda citrifolia, a tropical shrub of the coffee family spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors. The pungent fruit was historically a famine food, and parts of the plant were used in Polynesian medicine as a tonic. Today it is sold as juice, powders, supplements and in cosmetics.

name: Moringa
summary: A tropical tree whose seed oil and leaf extract show up in skin products, with antioxidant lab data but no skin-appearance trials.
lead: Moringa usually refers to Moringa oleifera, a fast-growing tree native to northern India and widely cultivated across the tropics, also known as the drumstick or horseradish tree. Its leaves, pods and seeds are eaten, and its seed oil (sometimes called ben oil) is used as a base in skin- and hair-care products.

name: Yuzu extract
summary: A citrus extract sold as a vitamin C botanical in Asian skin care, with lab antioxidant and pigment data but no skin trials.
lead: Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a tart, aromatic citrus fruit believed to have originated in central China and now grown mainly in Japan and Korea. Extracts of the peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products, usually marketed for their vitamin C and polyphenol content.

name: Horse oil
summary: An animal-derived emollient oil from Japanese and Korean skin care, backed by small formulation and cell studies only.
lead: Horse oil (ma-yu in Japanese and Korean cosmetic usage) is a fat rendered from horse tissue, used as an emollient ingredient in skin-care products, particularly in East Asia. Its fatty-acid profile, including linoleic and palmitoleic acids, has been described as similar to that of human skin lipids.

name: Starfish extract
summary: A K-beauty marine ingredient inspired by starfish regeneration, supported only by a zebrafish study and patents.
lead: Starfish extract is a preparation from the tissues of sea stars, listed in some Korean beauty products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient. Starfish are known for regrowing lost arms, and some researchers study their tissues for regenerative bioactive molecules.

name: Pig collagen
summary: A K-beauty mask protein with real surgical uses but no cosmetic trials, and a skin-penetration question the encyclopedia answers negatively.
lead: Pig (porcine) collagen is collagen protein derived from pig skin or connective tissue. In beauty it appears in sheet masks and creams, particularly in Korean products, and as a supplement; in medicine, porcine collagen is used in wound dressings and dental and surgical membranes.

name: Tea tree extract
summary: An Australian antibacterial botanical common in acne products; the oil has limited acne evidence, the extract has almost none.
lead: Tea tree extract and tea tree oil derive from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a plant native to eastern Australia. The oil is promoted for acne, dandruff and minor skin infections, and tea tree extract appears in cleansers and blemish products.

name: Acerola fruit extract
summary: Vitamin-C-rich tropical fruit extract used in beauty supplements; skin evidence exists only for multi-ingredient blends.
lead: Acerola fruit extract is a preparation made from the fruit of Malpighia emarginata, a tropical shrub native to the Neotropics and grown commercially in Brazil and other warm regions. The raw fruit is among the richest natural sources of vitamin C, with one nutrition table listing roughly 1,678 mg per 100 g.

name: Orchid extract
summary: Antioxidant K-beauty botanical from several orchid species; support is limited to lab, animal and patent material.
lead: Orchid extract refers to preparations from various orchid species used in cosmetics, most often marketed as antioxidant or anti-aging botanicals in Asian skincare. The orchid family (Orchidaceae) is very large, so the term covers different species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, with different chemistry.

name: Lotus extract
summary: Sacred-lotus botanical in K-beauty skincare; only two small human studies exist, both paired with green tea.
lead: Lotus extract is derived from the sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), an aquatic perennial whose seeds, rhizomes and leaves have long been used in food and in folk, Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine. It appears as an antioxidant botanical in K-beauty and other skincare products. The name is also applied to unrelated plants such as blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea), which has different chemistry.

name: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract
summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant botanical common in skincare; general health claims lack strong support and oral extracts carry liver warnings.
lead: Green tea leaf extract is a concentrate of polyphenols, mainly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), from unoxidized Camellia sinensis leaves. It is used in topical skincare as an antioxidant and in oral supplements.

name: Papaya extract
summary: Papaya-derived enzyme exfoliant botanical; no skin-appearance trials found and the FDA warned on topical papain drug products in 2008.
lead: Papaya extract is a preparation from the fruit, leaves, seeds or latex of Carica papaya. In skincare it is usually described as an enzyme exfoliant, because papaya latex is the source of the protein-digesting enzyme papain.

name: Oat extract
summary: Colloidal-oat soothing ingredient with FDA skin-protectant status; trials found for oat extracts are mostly dietary, not skin appearance.
lead: Oat extract in skincare usually means colloidal oatmeal or oat kernel extracts standardized for avenanthramides, phenolic compounds in Avena sativa that are studied as an anti-inflammatory component of oats. It is used in sensitive-skin, baby and sun-care products. The same name is also used for oat beta-glucan fiber extracts and green-oat extracts studied as foods or supplements, which are different preparations.

name: Cucumber extract
summary: A cooling, hydrating botanical in cleansers and eye products; popular imagery, but no controlled evidence for appearance benefits.
lead: Cucumber extract is a preparation made from the fruit, and sometimes the seeds, of Cucumis sativus, an annual vine of the gourd family that has been cultivated for at least 3,000 years . In skincare it is listed as a cooling, soothing botanical, and it is usually included in cleansers, toners, gels and eye products for its fresh-feel and mild, hydrating character rather than as an active ingredient.

name: Chamomile extract
summary: A calming flower extract in many soothing creams; lab data on inflammation and oral-use trials, but no skin-appearance trials.
lead: Chamomile extract is prepared from the flower heads of daisy-like plants in the Asteraceae family, most often German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) and Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) . It is used in herbal teas and in cosmetics, where it is a common soothing or calming botanical in creams, cleansers and masks.
